paras: The whitecap whipping of Black women near Myers, Missouri, was an attack in February 1903 in which a band the papers called "whitecaps" took Black women from a Black man's home near Myers, in eastern Howard County, whipped them, and ordered them to leave. The women had already been whipped and driven out of the town of Fayette, and after the second whipping they left the neighborhood the next day. Newspapers in St. Louis and Indianapolis carried it as a sequel to the Fayette whipping, and a Chariton County weekly reported it with approval.

Shortly before, several Black residents of Fayette, women among them, had been flogged and "directed to leave the city." According to the Chariton Courier, some of those driven out "found quarters" at the home of a Black man living near Myers. A later news note named the host as Elkin.

When their presence became known, the Courier wrote, "the good people of the neighborhood" ordered them to leave. Because they stayed, a party called on them intending to inflict "the same punishment as was administered to them at Fayette." The attack came at night, on what one report called "Tuesday night."

Accounts differ on who was whipped. The St. Louis and Indianapolis briefs and the Arizona item said two of the women were taken from the house and whipped. The Courier instead said the men in the group escaped and only one woman was captured and "given a severe whipping." In every version the victims were ordered to leave and went the next day, the St. Louis brief saying they departed from the county "in obedience to a command of the Whitecaps."

None of the attackers was named, though the Arizona item said the whitecappers were reputed to be "prominent farmers in that locality." No report of arrests, an inquest or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The incident first appeared on 22 February 1903 in the St. Louis Republic's "General Domestic" digest, and the same wording ran the next day among the Indianapolis Journal's "Telegraphic Brevities." Those one-sentence items called the women's attackers at Fayette "the citizens of Fayette," said the women were "whipped again," and added no comment. A differently worded note, naming Elkin and describing the attackers as "whitecappers," ran in the Arizona Weekly Journal-Miner on 4 March.

The fullest account came from the Chariton Courier of Keytesville on 6 March, which framed the attack as the work of "the good people of the neighborhood." It ended the item with the proverb "The way of the transgressor is hard," treating the whipping as deserved. All four reports of the Myers whipping found were in white newspapers; no Black-press account of this second attack was found.

Besides the number whipped, the timing is uncertain. The Arizona note of 4 March placed the whipping on a Tuesday night, but the St. Louis Republic had reported it on 22 February, so that Tuesday must fall before that date. The place name also appears as "Myas" in the St. Louis and Indianapolis briefs and as Myers in the other two reports.

reader.title: Whitecap whipping of Black women near Myers, Missouri
bases: A band the papers call 'whitecaps' or 'whitecappers' took Black women from a house near Myers at night, whipped them and ordered them out of the neighborhood (A5, A7, A8).

Three differently worded reports, a St. Louis digest brief (A5, reprinted A6), an Arizona news note (A7) and a Chariton County weekly (A8), agree that women driven out of Fayette were taken from a Black man's home near Myers, whipped and made to leave.

accounts.label: St. Louis digest brief
accounts.gist: Two of the women whipped by 'the citizens of Fayette' were taken from a Black man's home at 'Myas' and whipped again, then left the county at the Whitecaps' command.

accounts.label: Arizona news note
accounts.gist: Two women run out of Fayette were taken from Elkin's home near Myers on Tuesday night, whipped and ordered to leave, which they did next day; the whitecappers were said to be prominent farmers.

accounts.label: Chariton Courier (regional weekly)
accounts.gist: Neighbors ordered the Fayette exiles out; when they stayed, a party came to whip them; the men escaped, one woman was caught, severely whipped, ordered out, and left next day.

framing.detail: One-sentence digest items ('whipped again', 'In obedience to a command of the Whitecaps') with no comment, in the St. Louis Republic's 'General Domestic' and the Indianapolis Journal's 'Telegraphic Brevities'.
The Arizona item calls the attackers 'whitecappers' and reports they 'are said to be prominent farmers', without comment.
The Chariton Courier calls the attackers 'the good people of the neighborhood' and closes with 'The way of the transgressor is hard.'

versions.value: Two women taken from the house and whipped
The men escaped; one woman was captured and whipped

conflicts.note: A5 and A6 are one brief; A7 is a separate version. The Courier (A8) is the only regional account and the only one to mention men in the group, but it is also the latest; neither version is clearly better.
Same place; 'Myas' appears only in the shared digest brief.
The Tuesday must be one before 22 February; the 4 March item is a late reprint of an older note.

record_check.dossier: A Tuesday night in February 1903 before 22 February (reported in St. Louis on 22 February); 3 March was read off the 'Tuesday' in a late 4 March reprint
Unnamed Black women expelled from Fayette (two, or one per the Courier); host named Elkin
ordered_out, seizure, whipping; no pursuit is reported (the men 'made their escape')
unnamed 'whitecaps', said to be prominent local farmers
1903-02-22 (St. Louis Republic); four papers in all

info: A Tuesday night in February 1903, before 22 February (the St. Louis Republic carried it on 22 February); the record's 3 March is too late
At the home of a Black man (named Elkin in one report) near Myers ('Myas' in two briefs), in the eastern part of Howard County
Black women who had been whipped and run out of Fayette: two according to the briefs, one woman according to the Chariton Courier (the men with her escaped); none named
No crime is charged; the stated grievance was that people flogged and ordered out of Fayette had taken refuge near Myers and did not leave when ordered
'whitecaps' (A5), 'whitecappers' said to be 'prominent farmers in that locality' (A7), 'the good people of the neighborhood' (A8); none named
The victims left the neighborhood the next day (A7, A8); the briefs say they departed from the county (A5)

'Forced to Leave by Best Citizens': the earlier Fayette whipping of a man and two women by disguised white caps; no Myers incident.
Howard county notes: Fayette 'moral wave', six Black women fined; Fayette Advertiser disapproves of the whipping of women. No Myers incident.
Editorial mentions a 'Negro whipping bee at Fayette' (the parent event); nothing on Myers.
Editorial aside on 'white capping at Fayette' (placed in Kansas): four Black people, three women, tied to a tree and beaten; the parent event, not Myers.
